extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy of mathematics, philosophers of mathematical practice, and mathematicians interested in foundations and proof practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing mathematical proofs, explanations, diagrams, and other epistemic virtues in mathematical practice, as discussed in a handbook-style survey. Covers notions of explanatory power, rigor (formalizability), diagrammatic standards, and related epistemic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanatory power / mathematical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics can provide genuine explanations of empirical phenomena and of mathematical facts; explanatory power is an epistemic virtue of mathematical postulates and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Baker's cicada prime-period example and the honeycomb/honeybee example (honeycomb conjecture) illustrate mathematical facts that complete explanations of biological/evolutionary phenomena. Explanatory explanations are contrasted with merely descriptive roles; explanatory role can be used in an enhanced indispensability argument ('We ought to be committed to the entities postulated by the mathematics in question'). The literature attempts to characterize descriptive vs explanatory roles and to catalog many cases across physics, biology, medicine, and social sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for explanatory proofs (explanatoriness as a desideratum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs or methods that provide understanding or explanation are preferred over methods that merely establish truth without explaining why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Brumfiel rejects 'transcendental' proofs relying on a transfer principle because they 'may logically prove a result but they do not explain it, except for the special case of real numbers.' Mordell's remark about dissatisfaction with Euclidean proofs that do not 'throw light on the why and wherefore' illustrates the motivation to seek more explanatory proofs. Evaluations should attend to whether a proof illuminates origins, methods, and reasons, not just establishes correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor as formalizability (Standard View)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof is rigorous iff it can be translated into a formal derivation in some canonical deductive system (i.e., informal proofs should admit formal counterparts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mac Lane: 'a proof is a sketch, in sufficient detail to make possible a routine translation of this sketch into a formal proof.' Hamami's 'routine translation' decomposes this into: (i) make the informal argument explicit at a higher-level, (ii) unpack higher-level moves into basic steps, (iii) formalize those basic steps in a suitable system. Interactive theorem provers (Lean, Coq, Isabelle) instantiate this ideal and support formalization. Use formalizability as a benchmark: inability to formalize (e.g., independence phenomena) is taken as evidence the informal proof fails as a successful proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor pluralism / multiple models of rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor admits multiple legitimate models; no single model captures all functions and contexts of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tanswell's four models: (i) rigor as formality (Standard View), (ii) proofs as arguments and dialogues, (iii) the recipe model (proofs as guides to actions/activities), (iv) rigor as an intellectual virtue. Different models excel at different aims (tracking correctness, preserving content, enabling agreement, accommodating techniques like diagram use). Evaluation should select the model appropriate to aims and context rather than impose one universal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and social dimensions of rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments of rigor vary across subfields, historical periods, and pedagogical aims; rigor is a context-sensitive standard negotiated within mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ashton emphasizes variability of standards across contexts. Aberdein and Ashton analyze proof as argumentation that aims to persuade and withstand social scrutiny. Evaluators should consider field-specific norms, historical practices, and audience when judging rigor rather than applying a uniform criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence from (non-)formalizability as an epistemic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that an informal argument cannot be replicated by a formal analogue is taken as evidence that the informal proof is defective; conversely, partial formalizability supports confidence in informal proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence results show formalization limits (e.g., Continuum Hypothesis) and indicate when attempts to prove fail. Practically, mathematicians rely on the expectation that correct informal steps can be spelled out in detail and formalized; formal verification can serve as a hierarchical court of appeal in disputes even if rarely used routinely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs as dialogues / Prover–Skeptic model
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs can be conceptualized as dialogues between a prover and a skeptical opponent; rigor arises from meeting the skeptic's demands for necessary truth-preservation and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dutilh Novaes' Prover–Skeptic model treats deductive argument as semi-adversarial interaction: necessity of truth-preservation emerges from needing to convince skeptic; clarity of steps reflects cooperative goal of explanatory persuasion. Evaluations should consider whether a proof addresses imaginable skeptical challenges and makes steps sufficiently clear to persuade informed critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible inferential actions / argumentation-theoretic account of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some accounts (e.g., Larvor) propose that proofs are governed by permissible inferential actions in a broad conception of inference (not necessarily propositional); norms guiding a practice determine acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larvor's approach argues we cannot simply appeal to formal correctness to explain acceptance; instead, one must specify the normative rules (permissible actions) used in that practice. Evaluators should identify the locally negotiated inferential rules and judge conformity to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrammatic/visual rigor criteria (Manders' and Larvor's conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrammatic proofs can be rigorous provided certain structural conditions hold (e.g., Manders' textual/diagrammatic distinction; Larvor's three conditions for diagrammatic proof practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manders: Euclid's practice relies on textual (exact) vs diagrammatic (co-exact) components; distinguishing these controls inferential use. Larvor's three conditions to generalize beyond Euclid: (i) diagrams are easy to draw (require no special skill), (ii) the displayed information is non-metrical, and (iii) the inferences can be put into systematic mathematical relation with other inferential practices. Use these conditions to assess whether diagrammatic inferences count as rigorous in-context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams as systematic notational devices (definition and distinction from illustrations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are elements of notational systems (geometric-topological or two-dimensional) that are systematic — information and rules for correct use can be, at least potentially, spelled out — whereas illustrations are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Toffoli: diagrams are GT (geometric-topological) or two-dimensional representations; systematicity is crucial. Evaluators should check whether the diagram's information content and allowable manipulations are regulable and reproducible, not merely heuristic illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram efficacy: faithful representation and 'free rides'
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams can be epistemically effective because they iconically represent relations, show relations rather than state them, and allow 'free rides' where spatial configuration exhibits properties not explicit in linguistic counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carter's 'faithful representation' notion: diagrams allow manipulations that track relations; Shimojima's 'free rides' and Shin's observations about multiple readability (e.g., Peirce's existential graphs) show diagrams can make equivalences or relations manifest without complex parsing. When evaluating, consider whether a diagram provides such representational benefits and whether those benefits legitimately contribute to the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams as essential tools in some proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: In some areas (e.g., topology, knot theory), diagrams are essential to reasoning and proof, supporting epistemic actions not easily captured in linear sentential proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Toffoli and Giardino: knot and arrow diagrams support dynamic manipulations and epistemic actions. Corfield and others argue diagrams can be essential for certain proofs. Assessors should recognize domain-specific practices where diagrammatic manipulations constitute core inferential steps and evaluate whether those steps meet the community's rigor criteria (and whether formal counterparts can, in principle, be given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal diagrammatic systems and integration with formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to design formal systems faithful to diagrammatic argumentation (e.g., Mumma's Eu system, Avigad/Dean/Mumma work) that integrate diagrams into formal proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of such formal systems supports the claim that diagrammatic reasoning can be made rigorous; evaluators may consider whether the diagrammatic practice in question admits faithful formalization as evidence toward rigor or acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic virtue: purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity is an epistemic virtue discussed in the literature (one of the virtues alongside explanation, rigor, and visualizability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purity interacts with explanatory aims (e.g., debates over purity and explanation). References include Arana (2024) and Arana & Mancosu (2012). Evaluations may consider whether results/proofs respect concerns of conceptual or methodological purity appropriate to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic virtue: visualizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualizability (visual/diagrammatic clarity) is treated as an epistemic virtue that contributes to understanding and explanatory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the four focal virtues (purity, explanation, rigor, visualizability). Assessment should note whether visualization aids understanding legitimately and whether visualization-based inferences meet domain standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other epistemic virtues (simplicity, beauty, economy, depth, naturalness, fruitfulness, transferability, fitness, motivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of additional epistemic virtues are relevant when evaluating mathematical work: simplicity, beauty, epistemic economy, depth, naturalness and fruitfulness of definitions/concepts, transferability, fitness, and motivational features of proofs and concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These virtues interact with the four discussed in detail. References include Kossak & Ording (simplicity), Cellucci and others (beauty), Panza (epistemic economy), Gray & Lange (depth), Heuer et al. (naturalness/fruitfulness), and Raman-Sundström (transferability/fitness). Evaluations should consider how these virtues manifest (e.g., simpler proofs that illuminate may be preferred) but recognize trade-offs and context dependence.
